prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat moire bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model is the kind of result I trust most: a transparent mechanism (interlayer tunnelling renormalising the Dirac velocity to zero at a discrete magic angle) obtained analytically from a clean model, with a quantitative, falsifiable prediction. The 2018 experiments by Jarillo-Herrero and colleagues then found correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle, and many independent groups have reproduced them, so theory and experiment form one coherent discovery. It has created a new platform in which interaction strength is tuned by a twist angle and a gate voltage, which gives a controlled setting for strongly correlated physics, and it links condensed-matter theory with experiment in the way that a Physics prize should. The experimental discovery is now nearly a decade old and the basic picture has been checked across devices and groups, so the timing is reasonable.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and maturity of the interpretation. The mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, so the prize would honour the flat-band prediction and the observation of the phases rather than a fully understood phenomenon. Credit is also crowded: earlier continuum and commensurate-angle work (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto, Suarez Morell and others), the lead experimental authors of the 2018 papers (Cao, Fatemi), and the early independent experimental groups (Dean, Yazdani, Young, Efetov and others) all have arguable claims, and a three-person cap with a postdoc-level theory co-author is a genuine difficulty. Device-to-device variability from twist-angle disorder is a further caveat. If the committee judges the credit set unsound, the optical lattice clock candidate B029 is a much cleaner two-name configuration.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first: a measurement advance at 1e-18 with exceptional clarity of metric, and the field-opening impact for geodesy, constants and the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree that the clock is a very strong and mature candidate, and I ranked it second myself. The attribution of Katori (magic wavelength) and Ye (1e-18 systematics, many-body clock) is cleaner than for moire graphene. Where I disagree is on weight: the clock is a refinement of the ruler that the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize largely created, whereas twisted bilayer graphene opens a new regime of matter that was not accessible before. I would call the clock a close alternative and not a preferred prize, and I do not think the cleaner credit set alone should decide the matter.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle graphene first because it is a theory prediction followed by a decisive experiment, producing new quantum behaviour in a material, and he flags that Cao and Fatemi are not credited.
responses.response: I share this view and add the reason it appeals to me: the flat band follows from a simple mechanism that can be derived analytically, so the discovery is not only a phenomenon but an understood one at the single-particle level. I agree the omission of Cao and Fatemi is real; but the Nobel rules limit the prize to three, and the Bistritzer-MacDonald-Jarillo-Herrero set is the one that tracks the prediction and the group that led the discovery. I would resist your proposal in B016 to drop Mele while keeping Hasan, because that choice is the harder attribution problem.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the NV-centre work first and proposes only Wrachtrup and Jelezko, and for B031 she suggests testing whether a two-person experiment-plus-prediction pair (Jarillo-Herrero and MacDonald) is cleaner than three.
responses.response: I take the two-name suggestion seriously and it is a defensible fallback. But Bistritzer is the first author of the paper that contains the magic-angle prediction and the mechanism, and I would not leave out the person who did the calculation because he was a postdoc at the time; the committee has credited junior first authors before when the idea was theirs. On B001, I find the NV-centre work scientifically solid and well reproduced, but its main impact is as a tool and sensor, and I would want a clearer statement of what physics it discovered before ranking it above a new regime of correlated matter.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the gamma-ray burst afterglow discovery first, as an instrument-enabled discovery that settled a thirty-year debate, and ranks the Higgs experimental work third because the experimental side has never been honoured.
responses.response: The GRB result is a real discovery from nature, but I have two concerns: the credit set leaves out van Paradijs, who died, and several others who identified the optical counterpart, and the BeppoSAX team is large. For the Higgs I ranked it only sixth. The physics is beyond doubt, but the object of recognition would be the conception and construction of detectors by collaboration leaders, and the discovery of the boson itself involved thousands of people and also the accelerator builders. I do not think the 2013 theory prize creates an obligation to reward the experiment through three leaders, and I am not persuaded that the credit can be made defensible.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the foundation of superconducting quantum processors, a natural successor to the 2025 prize, while noting that dropping one of four names is a judgement call and flagging his closeness to the community.
responses.response: I accept that circuit QED is scientifically strong and widely reproduced. My reservation is the proximity to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, which Kroll also raises, and the four-name problem (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf, Girvin) that none of us has resolved: the opening ballots split between dropping Girvin and dropping Blais. That disagreement within the committee suggests that the credit is less settled than for the moire work. I appreciate that you flagged your own closeness to the community, and I would weigh B004 above its current support only if the committee can agree on the three.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the superconducting mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene is still open, and will treat the flat-band prediction plus the observation of the phases as a sufficient prize-level discovery.
Whether Bistritzer should be credited alongside MacDonald, and how much weight to give the earlier theory and the other early experimental groups.
How the committee weighs the clean two-name optical clock configuration against the broader but more contested moire platform.
My recollection of the exact priority details for the twisted-bilayer experiments and for the earlier theory has not been independently checked.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no known collaboration with any credited candidate. I note only that I sit in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Johansson and Olsson, whose fields touch B004 and B001, and I have therefore weighed their arguments on those candidates on their merits.
